clue.text: Greek scholar in charge, in form first

parts.note: a form is a school class or year group
1ST, the short form of first, written with I for the figure 1

explanation.surface: A classroom swot leads the class in Greek and has been put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Pieces run in the order given: CLASS, then IC, then 1ST read as IST.
explanation.definitionFit: A classicist studies ancient Greek and Latin, so a Greek scholar is a fair example.

clue.text: Updike theme, earlier used with the French

explanation.surface: A literary critic notes a subject John Updike borrowed, a word the French used first.
explanation.walkthrough: The Coup (1978) is John Updike's novel about a military takeover in a fictional African state; the word itself is French, a blow or stroke, long used in French phrases before English took it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Updike's novel takes a sudden seizure of power as its subject, and the term for such a seizure is a borrowing from French usage.

clue.text: End of church seen in gaps, easily

indicators.note: seen in says the letters can be spotted running inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: The east end of a church shows through gaps in the walls without difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the rounded or polygonal recess at the east end of a church, usually behind the altar.

clue.text: A particularly venomous Sayers offering

parts.note: reads as a nasty dose served by Dorothy L. Sayers, but points to the title of her 1930 Lord Peter Wimsey mystery about an arsenic murder

explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L. Sayers wrote the detective novel of this title, in which Harriet Vane is tried for a lethal arsenic dosing.

clue.text: Keats said that the Nile was this of the Pyramid and Crocodile

definitions.text: Keats said that the Nile was this of the Pyramid and Crocodile

parts.words: Keats said that the Nile was this of the Pyramid and Crocodile
parts.note: a quotation clue: the sonnet To the Nile hails the river as the leading lord of the Pyramid and Crocodile

explanation.definitionFit: Keats's sonnet To the Nile opens by addressing the river as head or ruler of the Pyramid and Crocodile.

clue.text: Calling for Connolly alter ego

parts.note: Cyril Connolly wrote The Unquiet Grave as Palinurus, the helmsman of Aeneas's ship, so the trade of that pseudonym is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: Palinurus, whose name Connolly borrowed, was the pilot at the helm of Aeneas's ship in the Aeneid.

clue.text: Declines, like Stevenson's sea

explanation.surface: A reader notes that interest falls away, as the tide does in Robert Louis Stevenson.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ebb-Tide is a novel by Robert Louis Stevenson (with Lloyd Osbourne); the sea in that title falls back.
explanation.definitionFit: To decline is to fall away or diminish; the retreating sea of Stevenson's title The Ebb-Tide flows back out.

clue.text: Most prolific writers, post 1938

parts.note: reads as the busiest authors of recent times, but means the pens László Bíró patented in 1938, the commonest writing tools since

explanation.definitionFit: Bíró's rolling-tip pen, patented in 1938, became the most widely used writing instrument in the world.

clue.text: I cheer a dead man's-,/Never ask me whose."(A.E. Housman)

definitions.text: I cheer a dead man's-,/Never ask me whose."(A.E. Housman)

parts.words: I cheer a dead man's-,/Never ask me whose."(A.E. Housman)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Is My Team Ploughing in A Shropshire Lad, where the living friend now comforts the dead man's girl

explanation.definitionFit: In Housman's poem the speaker now comforts the dead lad's beloved, the girl he courted.

clue.text: Rather like the quality of mercy — that's natural

definitions.text: Rather like the quality of mercy

explanation.surface: Portia's mercy speech is evoked to praise something unforced.
explanation.walkthrough: Portia in The Merchant of Venice says 'The quality of mercy is not strained'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercy in Portia's speech is not forced or constrained, and something unforced is natural and easy.

clue.text: An afternoon with William Boyd

parts.note: reads as a social date with the novelist, but points to the colour in the title of his 1993 novel set in 1930s Los Angeles

explanation.definitionFit: William Boyd's novel Blue Afternoon names an afternoon by this colour.

clue.text: Eliot characters from Irving's somnolent depression?

definitions.text: Eliot characters from Irving's somnolent depression?

parts.words: Eliot characters from Irving's somnolent depression?
parts.note: Washington Irving's Sleepy Hollow is a drowsy valley, so its inhabitants would be men of the hollow, which names an Eliot poem

explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's 1925 poem names its empty figures this way, and residents of Irving's Sleepy Hollow would fit the same phrase.

clue.text: Not a biography of Steve Davis by Ray Cooney

definitions.text: Not a biography of Steve Davis by Ray Cooney

parts.words: Not a biography of Steve Davis by Ray Cooney
parts.note: the phrase sounds like a snooker title for the champion Davis, who pots balls, but it is the name of Ray Cooney's farce, a tea-making saying

explanation.definitionFit: Ray Cooney's farce takes its title from the tea-making habit of adding an extra spoonful to the teapot.

clue.text: Moliere had him say that there was nothing dis honourable in sharing with Jupiter

definitions.text: Moliere had him say that there was nothing dis honourable in sharing with Jupiter

parts.words: Moliere had him say that there was nothing dis honourable in sharing with Jupiter
parts.note: in Molière's comedy the Theban general whose wife Jupiter seduced in disguise is told that sharing with a god brings no shame

explanation.definitionFit: Molière's 1668 comedy is named after the Theban general whose wife Alcmene was seduced by Jupiter in his likeness.

clue.text: Shakespeare's Christopher becomes spear-carrier, urgently

indicators.note: a carrier holds something within it, so the tinker's name takes the spear inside

parts.note: Christopher Sly is the drunken tinker of the Induction to The Taming of the Shrew
a trident is a three-pronged spear

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's drunken tinker is promoted to a walk-on soldier and acts with urgency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spear-carrier' reads as a theatre walk-on, but split it: 'spear' supplies letters and 'carrier' is the container signal, so the tinker's name holds the weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Stridently means in a loud, insistent manner, close to pressingly or urgently.

clue.text: Psalm met a strange modification of words

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of the preceding words are put into an odd new order

explanation.surface: A psalm meets an odd change in its wording.
explanation.definitionFit: Metaplasm is a grammatical term for altering a word by adding, removing or transposing letters or sounds.

clue.text: Part of chorus of praise for Handel

definitions.text: Part of chorus of praise for Handel

parts.words: Part of chorus of praise for Handel
parts.note: points to the shout of praise in the famous chorus of Handel's Messiah, spelt in an older form

explanation.definitionFit: The Messiah's great chorus repeats this Hebrew cry meaning praise the Lord.

clue.text: Danish poet, followed by English, turns out to be German

parts.note: Piet Hein was a Danish poet, famed for his short verses called grooks

explanation.surface: A Danish poet is unmasked as German once English is added.
explanation.walkthrough: Piet Hein plus E gives the German poet Heinrich Heine.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinrich Heine was a nineteenth-century poet from Düsseldorf, so German stands for him as a nationality.

clue.text: Nineteenth-century heroine from the idiom of schwyzerdiitsch

indicators.note: from says the letters come out of the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: A Swiss storybook girl is plucked from the local Swiss German dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: Schwyzerdütsch is Swiss German, fitting Johanna Spyri's Alpine heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Johanna Spyri's 1880 Swiss novel has the orphan girl of the Alps as its title character.

clue.text: Subsequent connection for Scottish novelist

parts.note: a link is a connection
subsequent means coming later

explanation.surface: A further tie is found to a writer from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go in the reverse of the clue's order: LINK, then LATER.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Linklater was an Orkney-raised writer of novels such as Juan in America.

clue.text: Clothe Lector in Fowlesian disguise as compiler

indicators.note: disguise means the letters of the words appear rearranged, and the Fowles nod hints at his novel's title

explanation.surface: Dressing Hannibal Lecter in a costume from a John Fowles novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Collector is John Fowles's first novel; the anagram is the novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A collector gathers and assembles items, just as a compiler puts material together.

clue.text: Xenophon commanded his posthumous katabasis

parts.note: Xenophon's Anabasis tells of the Ten Thousand's march inland for the Persian prince; after the prince fell, Xenophon led the retreat to the sea

explanation.definitionFit: Cyrus the Younger hired the Greek mercenaries and died at Cunaxa, after which Xenophon led their march home.

clue.text: One shoemaker in Thackeray work largely devoted to them?

definitions.text: One shoemaker in Thackeray work largely devoted to them?

parts.words: One shoemaker in Thackeray work largely devoted to them?
parts.note: an old word for a cobbler is also the subject of Thackeray's Book of ..., which mocks social climbers

explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant a cobbler or shoemaker's apprentice, and Thackeray's book is about social pretenders of this kind.

clue.text: Euphuistic writer repeatedly employs literary ends

indicators.note: repeatedly says the picked pair is written down twice in a row
ends picks the first and last letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A florid author keeps using literary flourishes.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lyly's Euphues (1578) gave English the word euphuism for an ornate prose style.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lyly's ornate prose romance Euphues gave its name to an elaborate style of writing.

clue.text: Elusive chap starts yarn expected to impress

indicators.note: starts picks the opening letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: A hard-to-pin-down man begins a tale meant to impress listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti, or abominable snowman, is a creature of Himalayan legend that famously eludes searchers.

clue.text: Some sacrifices had to be made for this art

definitions.text: Some sacrifices had to be made for this art

parts.words: Some sacrifices had to be made for this art
parts.note: sounds like an artist's personal dedication, but means the practice of divining from the offerings slain at the altar

explanation.definitionFit: Hieromancy is divination by examining sacrificial offerings, so the art needed victims slain.

clue.text: They dislike motion

parts.note: reads as people who hate movement, but motion is a proposal in a debate and these are the votes against it

explanation.definitionFit: Votes cast against a proposal in a debating chamber express opposition to the motion.

clue.text: Athens body organized to produce Frayn play down

indicators.note: organized says the letters of the words before it are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A Greek city council is set up to stage a play by Michael Frayn.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sandboy is Michael Frayn's 1971 play; 'down' sits off the definition as a wry nod to the phrase happy as a sandboy.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Frayn's 1971 stage comedy bears this title.
